Cloudflare Built a Browser in 12 Weeks. AI Agents Wrote Most of It

Last updated: August 10, 2026
By SarahJones
Share
10 Min Read
Listen to audio version of this article
Sponsored by
0:00 / 8:06
Instaread

 Cloudflare released Kitesurf on August 6, a  web browser with no tabs, no address bar, no extensions and no settings — because none of those things matter to the  software it was built for. It’s a browser for AI agents, and the first commit was in May.

Contents
First: what is a browser, actually?Why agents need something differentHow it was built, which is the actual storyThe numbersTrying it, and what breaksWhere this goes

Twelve weeks from nothing to a working browser passing 215,000 web standards tests. That timeline is only possible because of how it was built, which is the part of this announcement worth reading twice.

TestingPrivacy Web Browsers

First: what is a browser, actually?

Skip this section if you already know. It matters for the rest.

When you open a web page, your browser does roughly five jobs. It fetches the files — HTML, CSS, images, fonts, JavaScript. It parses the HTML into a Document Object Model, a tree structure representing the page. It applies CSS to work out how everything should look. It runs any JavaScript, which can modify that tree. Then it rasterizes the result: turning the computed layout into actual pixels on your screen.

- Advertisement -

Chrome, Firefox and Safari do all five, plus an enormous amount more. Smooth 60-frames-per-second scrolling. Tab management. Extension APIs. Password syncing. Video playback. Hardware-accelerated 3D graphics. Decades of accumulated compatibility work so that a page written in 2004 still renders.

TestingPrivacy Web Browsers

That last part is why browsers are among the most complex software humans build, and why almost nobody attempts a new engine.

Why agents need something different

Here’s the mismatch Cloudflare identified. An AI agent browsing the web needs jobs one through four — fetch, parse, style, execute — because that’s how it reaches the content. It barely needs job five, and it needs almost none of the extras.

Advertisements

As Cloudflare puts it, AI doesn’t care about tabs, themes, extensions or syncing across devices. It cares about token count, context windows, scalability, performance and cost. Structured machine-readable content matters; pixel-perfect rendering and smooth scrolling don’t. An agent is fine if the CSS parsing is slightly off.

But when you run an agent on Chromium, you pay for all of it anyway. Every browser instance carries the full weight of software designed for a human who might open twenty tabs and watch a video in one of them.

- Advertisement -

Cloudflare’s argument is that this cost has a gatekeeping effect: browser overhead is so high that giving every agent its own instance becomes prohibitively expensive, which restricts large parts of the web to only the most sophisticated and costly models and locks out everything else.

There’s also a security dimension. Your laptop browser assumes you’re mostly visiting sites you chose. An agent is pointed at whatever a task demands — arbitrary code from arbitrary origins. Cloudflare built Kitesurf assuming every page load is untrusted input, and every session starts fresh. Prompt injection and tool safety are the threats that matter here, not the ones Chrome was designed around.

How it was built, which is the actual story

Cloudflare says the idea of building a browser had come up internally every few months for years and been shelved every time. What changed was that WebAssembly support in Workers matured alongside primitives like Dynamic Workers, SQLite-backed Durable Objects and worker-to-worker RPC — at the same moment agents made a lightweight browser genuinely necessary.

The starting point was Obscura, an open-source headless engine written in Rust with no Chrome, no Node.js and no dependencies. Cloudflare tried porting it to Workers with an AI agent’s help. It didn’t work well at first. Once the team gave the agent a solid plan and a clear definition of success — detailed enough for it to loop endlessly and ask questions when needed — it worked.

The development method is the interesting bit. The Web Platform Tests suite, which measures conformance to W3C standards, became the goalposts.  Cloudflare curated which features to assign to agents and in what order, letting humans focus on architecture and reviewing the agents’ approaches while agents ground through conformance work against a measurable target.

That’s a genuinely instructive pattern. Not “AI wrote our code” but “we found a domain with an exhaustive automated success criterion and pointed agents at it.” Browser standards conformance is unusually well suited to that, because someone already wrote hundreds of thousands of tests defining correct behaviour.

Underneath, it’s Rust compiled straight to WebAssembly via wasm-bindgen, avoiding emulation layers. HTML and CSS parsing use parts of Blitz and Stylo — the latter being Firefox’s CSS engine. Text shaping runs through Parley. JavaScript eval, which Workers doesn’t support natively for security reasons, is handled by Boa JS, an ECMAScript engine written in Rust — a runtime running on top of a runtime, which Cloudflare openly calls suboptimal but says works.

The architecture splits into three parts: an Engine holding session state and speaking Chrome DevTools Protocol, a stateless PageScript that parses and executes each page in its own isolate, and a stateless PageRenderer that turns the result into pixels. A separate SandboxOutbound worker is the only component permitted to touch the network at all.

The numbers

Cloudflare benchmarked medians of five runs across a 14-URL corpus against a warm Chromium pool.

RegisteringCustom Web Domain Names

Kitesurf loses on the clock and Cloudflare says why: a just-in-time compiler that has already seen the page beats a cold  software renderer, with most of the gap in rasterization and image encoding.

Worth being precise about what the 3–7× figure means, because it’s being reported loosely. Cloudflare’s claim is that Kitesurf uses 3–7× less CPU and memory — the resources that drive your bill — and that this lowers costs for both Cloudflare and its customers. The company has not published a 3–7× cost reduction. Resource efficiency and billed cost are related, not identical.

Trying it, and what breaks

Kitesurf is free during beta through Browser Run, behind per-account limits. If you already use Puppeteer, Playwright, chrome-remote-interface, or any agent speaking MCP and CDP, it works — add browser=kitesurf to the endpoint.

There’s also a playground at kitesurf. cloudflare.app where you can point it at any URL. Cloudflare injected Chrome DevTools into that UI, so you can inspect the DOM, read console messages, and watch network activity. The Memory panel reports the WebAssembly footprint of each isolate, which is an unusually honest thing to expose.

It currently renders TodoMVC across five frameworks, Wikipedia, Hacker News, Cloudflare’s blog and much of its dashboard. It also runs Doom, which Cloudflare notes is the real completion criterion for any software project.

RegisteringCustom Web Domain Names

What it can’t do: video playback, WebGL, bot-challenge handshakes requiring real TLS fingerprints, or long authenticated sessions needing persistent state. For any of those, Cloudflare says use Browser Run’s Chromium default. The practical advice is to test your specific target sites in the playground first, because compatibility varies page by page in ways no summary can predict.

Where this goes

Cloudflare plans to open source Kitesurf so customers can deploy their own instances. No date given.

That matters more than the beta does. A cheap, auditable, self-hostable browser engine for agents is a different proposition from a managed service on one vendor’s platform — particularly for teams with data-residency constraints, which includes a lot of Indian enterprises working under sectoral data rules.

The larger point is that the web is starting to fork. For thirty years, browsers were built on the assumption that a human sits at the other end. That assumption is now wrong for a growing share of traffic, and Kitesurf is one of the first serious attempts to build for the other reader. Expect more of them.
